summary:
Same-sex conduct is criminalised in Cameroon under Article 347-1 of the penal code, which carries up to five years' imprisonment, and the 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations. Cameroon is one of 31 African countries that criminalise them, and reporting places it among the states worldwide that prosecute consensual same-sex conduct most aggressively. Prosecutions have rested on appearance and presentation rather than on observed conduct: arrests on grounds of effeminacy or dress have produced sentences ranging from six months to five years.

Trans women have been convicted on these provisions. In February 2021 the trans woman Shakiro and her friend Patricia were arrested in Douala in a restaurant for wearing women's clothing and were convicted of attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failure to carry identification. On 12 May 2021 a Douala court sentenced each to five years, the maximum statutory term, and a fine of 200,000 CFA francs; both had been detained since February 2021 and were released pending appeal after five months. Their lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu described the judgment as a political decision with no proof of any act. Shakiro subsequently left Cameroon to claim asylum abroad.

Earlier cases follow the same evidentiary pattern. Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome were jailed for five years in November 2011 after being seen in women's clothing and ordering Baileys, with the trial judge citing their dress, speech and drink as proof of homosexuality; an appeals court acquitted both on 9 January 2013, with Amnesty welcoming the outcome and lawyer Alice Nkom stating that the conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts. Jean-Claude Roger Mbede was arrested in 2011 for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance and served a three-year sentence at Kondengui Central Prison. In November 2011 three young men were sentenced to five years for oral sex in a parked car.

Human Rights Watch documented a marked rise in violence against LGBTI people in 2022: from 9 March that year, security forces arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven, all of whom had also been attacked by groups, over alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity, and gendarmes beat two detainees. The organisation's assessment is that the criminalisation statute permits both civilians and security forces to abuse LGBTI people without consequence. A US State Department human rights report recorded harassment and extortion of gay and lesbian people by law enforcement, including false allegations used to extort money.

Online contact is separately criminalised. The Law on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime (Law No. 2010/012, Article 83(1)) penalises online same-sex sexual propositions with one to two years' imprisonment and fines of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, doubled where intercourse followed. In May 2005 the government threatened forced medical examinations to 'prove' homosexual activity among eleven men arrested at a nightclub on suspicion of sodomy, a coercive use of health services rather than care.

Cameroon has no legal gender recognition procedure and no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation; failure to carry identification was charged alongside the anti-homosexuality counts in the 2021 case. Detention conditions reported by prisoners accused of homosexuality are severe, with Douala's main prison described as hell.

No Cameroonian visa policy, entry-refusal rule or border-admission procedure for LGBTQ travellers is described in the available sources. The nearest material concerns outbound movement: in July 2010 the United Kingdom granted a gay Cameroonian man the right to claim asylum, prompting Minister of Communication Issa Tchiroma Bakary to argue that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private activities; and in August 2011 a gay Cameroonian man was granted temporary immigration bail after Air France refused to carry him to Yaoundé. Cameroonian border screening of arriving travellers on gender-identity grounds is not documented.
tangentialFactors:
Criminalisation shapes the wider environment for everyone perceived as gender-nonconforming. In 2006 tabloids published the names of at least 50 prominent people alleged to be homosexual, boosting circulation and drawing criticism from the state communication council for invasion of privacy; President Paul Biya publicly urged respect for privacy while the state continued prosecuting people accused of homosexual activity. Beatings of gay and transgender people in public are reported as common.

On 30 June 2024 President Biya's daughter Brenda Biya came out as lesbian on Instagram, provoking national backlash while also giving LGBTQ Cameroonians a measure of hope. Public statements by officials have elsewhere minimised the risk: Issa Tchiroma Bakary's 2010 response to a UK asylum grant asserted that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private acts, a claim contradicted by the prosecution record.

The regional comparison matters for expectation-setting. Cameroon's maximum five-year penalty under Article 347-1 sits within a group of 31 African states criminalising same-sex conduct, but its frequency of prosecution and its use of dress, speech and beverage orders as evidence distinguish it from jurisdictions where the statute is rarely enforced. Detention periods before appeal can be long, as in the five months Shakiro and Patricia spent in prison before release pending appeal.
localsOnly:
Residents face obligations that visitors do not in the same form: Cameroonian law requires citizens to carry identification, and failure to do so was prosecuted alongside the anti-homosexuality counts in the 2021 Douala case, adding a charge that can attach independently of any alleged sexual conduct.

The domestic support structure has been damaged. Alternatives-Cameroon, an LGBTQ organisation, shut down after a police raid, removing a base of services for residents. Few lawyers are willing to defend people accused in homosexuality cases; Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu are among the small number who have done so.

Online activity carries its own exposure for residents under Law No. 2010/012, Article 83(1), which punishes same-sex sexual propositions made online with one to two years' imprisonment and fines of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, doubled where intercourse followed. Media outing of named individuals has precedent, and residents arrested in nightclubs or restaurants have been subjected to threats of forced medical examination.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Cameroonian visa rule, entry-refusal criterion or border-admission procedure for LGBTQ or transgender travellers is sourced. The available material concerns outbound asylum and airline carriage rather than admission to Cameroon, and any entry screening on gender-presentation grounds remains unresolved.

Access to healthcare, HIV services and hormone medication for transgender visitors is not described in the sources. The only health-related finding is the 2005 government threat of forced medical examinations to establish homosexual activity among detained men.

No legal gender recognition, legal name change or identity-document marker procedure for Cameroon is documented in the sources; the absence of a sourced procedure should be read as unresolved rather than as a confirmed statutory prohibition. Equally unsourced are any youth-, school- or minor-specific provisions relating to gender identity, and the practical outcome of the 2021 appeal in Shakiro and Patricia's case beyond their release pending appeal and Shakiro's departure from the country.

Prison-conditions claims rest on prisoner accounts and reporting rather than on inspection records, and the extent to which Article 347-1 is charged in practice outside the documented cases cannot be quantified from the inventory.
